name: Tibetan Buddhism

quote.text: All the joy the world contains has come through wishing happiness for others. All the misery the world contains has come through wanting pleasure for oneself.
quote.source: The Way of the Bodhisattva 8.129, trans. Padmakara

quotes.source: Seven Points of Mind Training, 12th century

quotes.text: For as long as space endures, and for as long as living beings remain, until then may I too abide to dispel the misery of the world.

quotes.source: Seven Points of Mind Training, 12th century

quotes.text: Always maintain only a joyful mind.
quotes.source: Seven Points of Mind Training, 12th century

words.meaning: The awakened heart: the wish to awaken for the sake of all beings
words.usage: The motive that turns any act into practice.
Breathing in others’ pain, breathing out relief.
Fifty-nine short slogans for turning daily life into the path.
Literally "noble heart". Sanskrit: karuṇā.
The wish that others be happy. Sanskrit: maitrī.
The everyday greeting, and what people say at the New Year.
Translates the Sanskrit guru: one who is weighty with qualities.
A title of respect for a reincarnate or highly regarded teacher.
The Dalai Lama and the Karmapa are the best known.
Earned after some twenty years of study and debate.
One of the three jewels in which Buddhists take refuge.

words.meaning: The teaching; the truth of how things are
words.usage: Tibetan: chö.
Resting attention on the breath or an object. Sanskrit: śamatha.
Looking into the nature of mind once it is calm. Sanskrit: vipaśyanā.
Things lack fixed, independent existence. Sanskrit: śūnyatā.
Everything arises through causes and conditions.
Intentions shape habits, and habits shape a life.
Tibetan: khorwa, "going round".
Most famously between death and rebirth, but also this life, sleep and meditation.

words.meaning: Sacred syllables that protect the mind
words.usage: Recited aloud or silently, often counted on a mala.
Tibetans pronounce the last words "peme hung". Carved on stones across the Himalaya.
Used to count recitations.

words.meaning: A sacred circle; a model of an enlightened world
words.usage: Painted, built, or poured in coloured sand and then swept away.
A support for meditation, painted to strict proportions.
Walked around clockwise.

words.meaning: A monastery; a place of meditation
words.usage: Literally "solitary place".
Walking clockwise around a holy place as practice.
The horse printed on prayer flags, carrying good wishes on the wind.
Offered at greetings, partings and to teachers.
Giving away the good of what you have done.
Literally "great compassion".
Fifteen days of offerings, visits and sweet rice in late winter.

practices.name: Tonglen
practices.instructions: Sit quietly and rest for a minute in open stillness. Then breathe in a sense of heaviness, heat and darkness, and breathe out lightness, coolness and brightness, until the rhythm is steady. Now bring to mind someone who is suffering. Breathe in their pain with the wish that they be free of it; breathe out whatever would help: ease, courage, rest. Finally widen it to everyone in the same situation. Begin with your own discomfort if another person feels too much.
practices.why: Tonglen reverses the habit of pulling in what is pleasant and pushing away what hurts. It is the central practice of the lojong tradition, taught openly by Tibetan teachers to anyone.
variations: On-the-spot tonglen: three breaths when you meet suffering during the day.
Tonglen for yourself and everyone who feels as you do right now.
Tonglen for someone you find difficult.

practices.name: Mantra: Om Mani Padme Hum
practices.instructions: Recite the six syllables aloud or under your breath, one round of 108. If you have a mala, move one bead per recitation with your thumb. Let the sound be even and unhurried. As you recite, hold the wish that all beings be free from suffering.
practices.why: This is the mantra of Chenrezig, the bodhisattva of compassion. Tibetans of every school recite it while walking, working and turning prayer wheels. It needs no initiation.
variations: Twenty-one recitations whenever you wait in a queue.
Listen to a recording and join in.

practices.name: Mind-training slogan
practices.instructions: Take one slogan from the Seven Points of Mind Training and write it where you will see it. Read a short commentary on it. For the rest of the day, try to recall it at the moment it applies: when blamed, when praised, when irritated, when pleased with yourself.
practices.why: The slogans were passed on privately for generations before Geshe Chekawa taught them openly. They are deliberately short so they come to mind when needed.
variations: "Of the two witnesses, hold the principal one."

practices.name: Dedication of merit
practices.instructions: Before sleep, recall the good things you did today, however small, and rejoice in them. Then give them away: may whatever good came from this day help all beings be free from suffering. Name anyone you especially want to include.
practices.why: Every Tibetan practice session ends with dedication. Giving the merit away is said to protect it from being burned up by pride or anger.
variations: Dedicate the day to one person who is ill or grieving.
Light a candle as you dedicate.

practices.name: Calm abiding
practices.instructions: Sit upright and rest your attention lightly on the breath at the nostrils or belly. When you notice you have drifted, name it quietly ("thinking") and return, without scolding. Aim for gentle stability, not a blank mind. Ten minutes is enough; stop when attention gets tight.
practices.why: Shamatha, calm abiding, is the foundation in Tibetan Buddhism for the analytic and compassion practices that follow. A steady mind is the ground for the rest.
variations: Count breaths from one to ten and begin again.
Rest attention on a small object instead.

tasks.name: Read one Lojong slogan with a commentary
Offer a bowl of water
tasks.meta: Fresh each morning, emptied at dusk

tasks.name: Read a chapter of The Way of the Bodhisattva
Watch The Cup: young monks and a World Cup final
Journal: whose suffering did you notice today, and what did you do?
Explain emptiness in three sentences, then doubt them
Drink a cup of tea in silence and dedicate it to someone
Hang something colourful where the wind can move it
tasks.meta: A wish for everyone it touches

tasks.name: Make butter tea, or tea with milk and a pinch of salt
Wish three strangers well as they pass, silently
Spin a prayer wheel in your mind: one kind wish per turn, twenty turns
Light a candle or a small lamp and make one wish for all
tasks.meta: Butter lamps burn in every temple

tasks.name: Pause at the door and wish the street well

rules.text: Open the day by choosing your motivation
rules.why: The Dalai Lama describes starting each morning by shaping his motivation. What you intend at the start colours everything after.
A lojong slogan advises: do not talk about injured limbs. Dwelling on other people’s faults strengthens your own.
Water, light, food, time. Generosity is the first of the six perfections, and it starts small.

rules.text: Close the day by dedicating the good
rules.why: So that the day’s practice belongs to everyone, not to a private scoreboard.

rules.text: Leave empowerment practices to a teacher
rules.why: Deity yoga and other tantric methods are given by a qualified teacher within a relationship. They are not part of this Onda, and they are not a do-it-yourself project.
Keep texts and images off the floor and do not step over them. It is a small habit that shows how much a thing can mean to someone else.

art.title: The Wheel of Life

art.why: A map of the mind’s habits, held in the jaws of impermanence.

art.title: Potala Palace

eat.title: Momos
eat.creator: Steamed dumplings
eat.why: Vegetable or meat, with a sharp tomato chutney.

eat.title: Thukpa
eat.creator: Noodle soup
eat.why: What you eat when it is cold, which in Tibet is often.

eat.title: Tsampa
eat.creator: Roasted barley flour
eat.why: The staple of the plateau, kneaded with tea into a dough.

eat.title: Tingmo
eat.creator: Steamed bread
eat.why: Soft, layered and plain, for soaking up stew.

eat.title: Dresil
eat.creator: Sweet rice with butter and dried fruit
eat.why: Served at Losar for an auspicious start.

drink.title: Butter tea
drink.creator: Po cha
drink.why: Tea churned with butter and salt. More like broth than tea.

customs.title: Hang prayer flags
customs.creator: Lungta
customs.why: Outdoors and high up, so the wind carries the wishes. Do not let them touch the ground.

customs.title: Turn prayer wheels clockwise
customs.creator: Mani wheels
customs.why: Each turn counts as reciting the mantras rolled inside.

customs.title: Offer a khata
customs.creator: A white scarf
customs.why: Held in both hands and offered with a slight bow.

customs.title: Walk clockwise
customs.creator: Kora
customs.why: Around stupas, temples and holy mountains, keeping them on your right.

customs.title: Offer water bowls
customs.creator: Seven bowls on a shelf
customs.why: Filled each morning with clean water, a grain’s width apart, and emptied at dusk.

customs.title: Light a butter lamp
customs.creator: Or a candle
customs.why: An offering of light to dispel the darkness of ignorance.

games.title: Sho
games.creator: Dice game · Tibet
games.why: Two dice slammed down from a wooden cup onto a leather pad, with shells and coins as the track. Fast, loud and played with rhyming calls for the number you want.

games.title: Rebirth
games.creator: Board game · attributed to Sakya Pandita
games.why: A teaching game: a die moves you through the realms of existence, down to the hells or up through the stages of the path. It shows the Buddhist map of the cosmos at a glance.

games.title: Mig mang
games.creator: Board game · Tibet
games.why: The many-eyed game, a Tibetan relative of Go played on a smaller grid, with stones placed at the start.

festivals.title: Losar
festivals.creator: February or March
festivals.why: Tibetan New Year. Houses are cleaned, debts settled and prayer flags replaced. The first days are for family, monastery visits and good food.

festivals.title: Monlam Chenmo
festivals.creator: The weeks after Losar
festivals.why: The Great Prayer Festival, founded by Tsongkhapa in Lhasa in 1409. Monks gather for days of prayer, debate and butter sculpture.

festivals.title: Saga Dawa
festivals.creator: Full moon of the fourth Tibetan month, May or June
festivals.why: The month that marks the Buddha’s birth, awakening and passing. Good deeds are said to count many times over, and many people eat no meat.

festivals.title: Shoton
festivals.creator: August, in Lhasa
festivals.why: The yogurt festival. A giant painted scroll is unrolled on the hillside at Drepung at dawn, followed by days of opera and picnics.

places.title: Boudhanath
places.creator: Kathmandu, Nepal
places.why: A great white stupa and the heart of Tibetan life in exile. Join the stream of people walking round it clockwise at dusk.

places.title: Dharamshala
places.creator: Himachal Pradesh, India
places.why: Seat of the Dalai Lama and the Tibetan government in exile. The main temple, library and Tibet Museum are open to visitors.

places.title: Bodh Gaya
places.creator: Bihar, India
places.why: The place of the Buddha’s awakening. Tibetan pilgrims prostrate beside the Mahabodhi Temple through the winter months.

places.title: Jokhang
places.creator: Lhasa, Tibet
places.why: The holiest temple in Tibet, circled all day by pilgrims. Travel in Tibet needs a permit and an approved guide.

places.title: Samye
places.creator: Dranang, Tibet
places.why: The first monastery in Tibet, founded in the eighth century and laid out as a map of the Buddhist cosmos.

places.title: Mount Kailash
places.creator: Ngari, western Tibet
places.why: A peak sacred to four religions. Pilgrims walk the 52 kilometre circuit round it and no one climbs it.

ethics.title: Cherish others more than yourself
ethics.text: The root of the mind-training tradition: self-cherishing is the source of trouble, and cherishing others is the source of every good.
ethics.practice: In one choice today, deliberately take the lesser share.

ethics.title: Turn adversity into the path
ethics.text: When the world is full of harm, transform all mishaps into the way of awakening. Difficult people become your teachers of patience.
ethics.practice: Name today’s biggest irritation and thank it for what it lets you practice.

ethics.title: Dedicate merit to all beings
ethics.text: Whatever good you do, give it away at once, so that it belongs to everyone.
ethics.practice: Finish one good piece of work today and take no credit for it.

ethics.title: The six perfections
ethics.text: Generosity, ethical conduct, patience, joyful effort, concentration and wisdom: the training of a bodhisattva.
ethics.practice: Pick one of the six and practice it on purpose until evening.

ethics.title: Equalising self and other
ethics.text: Everyone wants to be happy and no one wants to suffer. On that point there is no difference between you and anyone else.
ethics.practice: With each person you meet, think: just like me, this person wants to be happy.

ethics.title: Do no harm
ethics.text: The Buddha’s summary: do no harm, do what is good, tame your own mind.
ethics.practice: Go a full day without killing anything, including insects.

philosophy.title: Emptiness
philosophy.text: Nothing exists on its own. Things arise in dependence on causes, parts and the mind that names them. This is not nothingness; it is why change is possible.
philosophy.practice: Pick an object and list what it depends on. Keep going.

philosophy.title: Interdependence
philosophy.text: Your food, clothes, language and life all come from others. The Dalai Lama calls compassion simply being realistic about this.
philosophy.practice: Trace one meal back through all the hands that made it possible.

philosophy.title: Impermanence
philosophy.text: Everything composed comes apart. Remembering it loosens grasping and gives the day urgency.
philosophy.practice: When something pleasant ends today, watch it go without reaching.

philosophy.title: Karma
philosophy.text: Actions leave traces. What you do, say and think shapes what you become, and intention matters most.
philosophy.practice: Before one action today, stop and check what you actually intend.

philosophy.title: Precious human life
philosophy.text: To be alive, free and able to practice is rare and will not last. Do not waste it.
philosophy.practice: List five freedoms you have that make practice possible.

philosophy.title: The nature of mind
philosophy.text: Beneath passing thoughts and moods, awareness itself is clear and open, like sky behind cloud.
philosophy.practice: For one minute, watch thoughts come and go without following any.

philosophy.title: The two truths
philosophy.text: Conventionally, things work as they appear. Ultimately, they are empty of fixed nature. Both are true at once.
philosophy.practice: Hold a strong opinion today and also see it as one view.

philosophy.title: Suffering has causes
philosophy.text: The four noble truths: there is suffering, it has causes, it can end, and there is a path.
philosophy.practice: When upset, look for the grasping or aversion underneath.

philosophy.title: Bodhicitta
philosophy.text: The resolve to wake up for the benefit of everyone. It is said to turn even small acts into gold.
philosophy.practice: Begin one ordinary task with the thought: may this be of use.

philosophy.title: The bardo of this life
philosophy.text: This life is itself an in-between. How you meet small endings now is practice for the large one.
philosophy.practice: At the end of the day, let it go completely before sleep.

Which practice changed you the most, and why?

intro: Tibetan Buddhism is the form of Buddhism that took root on the Tibetan plateau from the seventh century and spread across the Himalaya, Mongolia and, in the last sixty years, the world. Its daily heart is the deliberate training of compassion.

It grew from late Indian Buddhism, which reached Tibet in two waves. In the eighth century the king Trisong Detsen invited the abbot Śāntarakṣita and the tantric master Padmasambhava, and together they founded Samye, the first monastery. After a period of collapse, a second wave began in the eleventh century with the Bengali teacher Atiśa and the Tibetan translator Marpa. From these two transmissions come the four main schools: Nyingma, the "ancient" school that looks to Padmasambhava; Kagyu, the lineage of Marpa and the hermit-poet Milarepa; Sakya; and Gelug, founded by the scholar Tsongkhapa, to which the Dalai Lamas belong.

All four share a foundation. One begins by reflecting on the rarity of a human life, on impermanence, on action and its results, and on the unsatisfactoriness of grasping. On that ground stands the Mahāyāna ideal: the bodhisattva, who seeks awakening not for private peace but to be of use to every being. Its motive is bodhicitta, the awakened heart.

Tibet preserved and refined a set of methods for growing that heart. The best loved is lojong, mind training: fifty-nine pithy slogans written down in the twelfth century, such as "Be grateful to everyone" and "Drive all blames into one". With them goes tonglen, giving and taking, in which you breathe in the suffering of others and breathe out relief. These practices are taught publicly and need no initiation.

The tradition also holds Vajrayāna or tantric practices: visualisation, mantra and subtle-body yogas that are given by a teacher through empowerment and within a close relationship. They are not secret out of exclusiveness but because they are easy to misuse. This Onda does not include them.

Tibetan Buddhism today is practiced under pressure. Since 1959 the Dalai Lama and many of the great teachers have lived in exile, and the monasteries were rebuilt in India and Nepal. Approach this Onda as a guest. Learn from Tibetan teachers where you can, and let the practice be for others.

figures.name: Padmasambhava
figures.bio: Guru Rinpoche, the "second Buddha" of the Nyingma school, credited with establishing tantric Buddhism in Tibet.

figures.name: Śāntideva
figures.bio: Indian monk of Nālandā. Author of The Way of the Bodhisattva.

figures.name: Atiśa
figures.bio: Bengali master who came to Tibet in 1042 and carried the mind-training teachings.

figures.name: Marpa
figures.bio: Farmer and translator who made three journeys to India for teachings.

figures.name: Milarepa
figures.bio: Marpa’s student. After a youth of revenge he spent his life in mountain caves and taught in song.

figures.name: Geshe Chekawa
figures.bio: Wrote down the Seven Points of Mind Training and taught them openly.

figures.name: Tsongkhapa
figures.bio: Scholar and reformer. Founded Ganden monastery and the Gelug school.

figures.name: Patrul Rinpoche
figures.bio: Wandering Nyingma teacher who lived as a beggar and wrote The Words of My Perfect Teacher.

figures.name: Jamgön Kongtrul
figures.bio: Leader of the non-sectarian Rimé movement and author of the standard lojong commentary.

figures.name: Tenzin Gyatso, the 14th Dalai Lama
figures.bio: Spiritual leader of Tibetans. In exile since 1959. Nobel Peace Prize, 1989.

history.detail: King Songtsen Gampo unifies Tibet and marries princesses from Nepal and China, who by tradition bring Buddhist images. The Jokhang temple in Lhasa is founded and a Tibetan script is devised.

history.what: Samye, the first monastery, is founded
history.detail: Under King Trisong Detsen, with the abbot Śāntarakṣita and Padmasambhava. The first seven Tibetans are ordained.
After the assassination of King Langdarma, central rule breaks down and monastic Buddhism declines for more than a century.
Invited by a western Tibetan king, he teaches for twelve years. His students found the Kadam school, the source of lojong.
Marpa brings teachings from India; his student Milarepa practices in solitude and attracts followers. Gampopa organises their lineage as the Kagyu school.
The Sakya school later provides Tibet’s rulers under Mongol patronage.

history.what: The mind-training slogans are written down
history.detail: Geshe Chekawa, moved by the line "give all gain to others, take all loss on yourself", seeks out the teaching and sets it in seven points.
The Gelug school emphasises monastic discipline and a graded path of study.

history.what: The title Dalai Lama is first given
history.detail: The Mongol ruler Altan Khan confers it on Sonam Gyatso, counted as the third in the line.

history.what: The Fifth Dalai Lama becomes ruler of Tibet
history.detail: With Mongol support he unifies the country. Building of the Potala Palace begins in 1645.
Jamgön Kongtrul, Jamyang Khyentse Wangpo and others collect and preserve the teachings of all schools without sectarian bias.

history.what: The People’s Liberation Army enters Tibet
history.detail: The fifteen-year-old Dalai Lama assumes full political authority that year.

history.what: The Dalai Lama goes into exile
history.detail: After an uprising in Lhasa he crosses the Himalaya to India, followed by tens of thousands. A government in exile is established at Dharamsala.
Awarded to the Dalai Lama for his non-violent stance on Tibet.

concepts.text: The resolve to awaken for the sake of all beings.
concepts.detail: It has two aspects: the wish, and the actual training in the six perfections. Tibetans call it the wish-fulfilling jewel.

The points move from preliminaries, through the main practice of tonglen and of resting in openness, to turning hardship into the path, and end with lists of commitments and guidelines for daily life.

concepts.text: Giving and taking on the breath.
concepts.detail: You take in what you would normally avoid and send out what you would normally keep. The aim is to dissolve the armour around the heart, not to become ill on others’ behalf.

concepts.text: Things have no independent, fixed existence.
concepts.detail: The philosophy of Nāgārjuna, studied intensely in Tibet. Emptiness and compassion are called the two wings of a bird: neither works without the other.
Taking refuge in them is what makes someone a Buddhist. Tibetans add the lama as the one who makes the three accessible.

concepts.text: Reflections that turn the mind to practice.
concepts.detail: Precious human birth, impermanence and death, action and result, and the defects of cyclic existence.
Generosity, ethical conduct, patience, joyful effort, meditative concentration and wisdom.

concepts.text: A teacher recognised as the rebirth of a predecessor.
concepts.detail: The system began with the Karmapas in the thirteenth century. It gave Tibet a way to pass on spiritual authority without heredity.
Methods using visualisation, mantra and the subtle body, said to be swift and to depend on empowerment from a qualified teacher. Not included in this Onda.

concepts.text: The positive force of good action, given away.
concepts.detail: Merit is not a private bank account. Dedicating it to all beings is itself the practice of non-attachment.

facts.text: The Tibetan word for a Buddhist is nangpa, "insider": one who looks for the truth inside the mind.
Prayer flags come in five colours for the five elements, always in the same order: blue, white, red, green, yellow.
Monks may spend days making a sand mandala and then sweep it away in minutes, as a teaching on impermanence.
Tibetan monastic debate is physical: the challenger stands, shouts the question and claps one hand down on the other.
The title Dalai is Mongolian for ocean. Tibetans more often call him Kundun, "the presence".
Tsampa, roasted barley flour, is so central to Tibetan identity that Tibetans sometimes call themselves "tsampa eaters".
The lojong slogans were passed on privately before Geshe Chekawa taught them publicly in the twelfth century.
The mantra Om mani padme hum is carved into stones and stacked in walls, some hundreds of metres long, across the Himalaya.

glossary.meaning: The "great vehicle": Buddhism of the bodhisattva ideal.
The four main schools of Tibetan Buddhism.
The bodhisattva of compassion. Sanskrit: Avalokiteśvara.
A ritual in which a teacher authorises a student for a tantric practice.
The Indian hill town that is the Dalai Lama’s home in exile.

sensitivity.note: Tibetan Buddhism is a living tradition whose people have been in exile since 1959. This Onda uses only practices that Tibetan teachers offer publicly: tonglen, the compassion mantra and the mind-training slogans. Practice as a guest, and learn from Tibetan teachers where you can.
requiredCaveats: Tantric practices that require empowerment from a qualified teacher are not included and should not be improvised.
Prayer flags, images and texts are sacred objects, not decoration. Treat them with care.
If tonglen stirs up more than you can hold, return to simple breathing and seek guidance.
This content has not yet been reviewed by a Tibetan Buddhist teacher.
